name: Dexfenfluramine (Redux)
lead: Dexfenfluramine matters to appearance history because it was one of the most widely prescribed prescription routes to fat loss in the mid-1990s: people took it to lose weight, which makes faces and bodies look leaner, and its withdrawal reshaped how later weight-loss drugs were evaluated for heart safety.

Dexfenfluramine, sold in the United States under the brand name Redux, is the dextrorotatory enantiomer of fenfluramine and was developed as a serotonin-acting appetite suppressant for obesity. It is structurally related to amphetamine but is described as lacking amphetamine-type stimulant effects.[1][2]

Interneuron Pharmaceuticals, co-founded by MIT researcher Richard Wurtman, developed the drug and licensed its patent to Wyeth-Ayerst Laboratories. The FDA approved it for weight loss in the mid-1990s, and approval was withdrawn in September 1997 after reports of cardiovascular harm, chiefly heart-valve disease and pulmonary hypertension.[1][5]

Controlled trials from the 1980s and 1990s examined long-term dexfenfluramine treatment in obesity,[4] and later pharmacology work linked the drug's cardiac and pulmonary harms to activation of the serotonin 5-HT2B receptor by its active metabolite.[5][6] It is no longer marketed, and it appears in appearance-focused discussion mainly as a historical diet drug and as half of the "fen-phen" combination.
infobox: Withdrawn; unscheduled in the US; Brazil lists it as prohibited

paras: Dexfenfluramine was approved as an adjunct to diet and exercise for obesity in adults. Its only recognised use was weight reduction through reduced appetite.[1][7]

The Lancet published an international trial of long-term dexfenfluramine in obesity in 1989,[4] and reviews of serotonergic agents describe sustained serotonin signalling in the hypothalamus as a basis for appetite control, with 5-HT2C and 5-HT1B receptors implicated.[7] Reviews also note that serotonin-acting drugs of this kind produced clinically meaningful weight loss over a year or longer.[7]

A set of 1998 studies in the New England Journal of Medicine then examined heart-valve findings in people who had taken appetite-suppressant drugs, including a placebo-controlled assessment of dexfenfluramine and sustained-release dexfenfluramine, and a population-based study of valve regurgitation.[8][9][10]

Separate research used a dexfenfluramine challenge together with PET imaging to investigate serotonin function in MDMA users (registered trial NCT01296802).[11] That work concerns serotonin neuroscience rather than weight loss.

Smaller trials examined how dexfenfluramine behaved in specific groups: drug therapy after very-low-calorie diets [19], blood glucose control in type 2 diabetes [20], and body-weight evolution after initial weight control [21]. A 1996 review in Drugs summarised its therapeutic use in obesity [22]. Pharmacokinetic work compared single intravenous and oral doses of dexfenfluramine and its metabolite dexnorfenfluramine in 10 obese and 10 non-obese volunteers [23].

Fenfluramine was introduced in the 1970s, sold modestly alone, and gained wide use after it was combined with phentermine in the regimen called fen-phen. According to Wikipedia, a University of Rochester trial in 1984 found about 8.4 kg of weight loss over 24 weeks with the combination versus about 4.4 kg with placebo, Wyeth introduced dexfenfluramine in 1995, and the FDA approved it in 1996 without a black-box warning that its medical officer had requested [12]. The term fen-phen was coined in 1994 when two researchers reported that the combination might reduce alcohol and cocaine cravings [12].

The drug was withdrawn because of heart-valve disease and pulmonary hypertension. Pharmacological studies report that the valve changes resemble those seen in carcinoid disease or with some ergot drugs, and propose that 5-HT2B receptor stimulation on valve cells, by the drug's metabolite, drives the cell proliferation involved.[5]

A 2002 Nature Medicine study reported that dexfenfluramine increases pulmonary hypertension risk in humans and that its active metabolite is a selective 5-HT2B agonist; it found a role for this receptor in the disease process.[6]

In August 1997 a Mayo Clinic paper in the New England Journal of Medicine described 24 people who took fen-phen and suggested a link to mitral valve dysfunction, and in September 1997 the FDA requested withdrawal of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine; Wikipedia reports about 30 percent of those who took the combination for up to 24 months had abnormal echocardiograms, versus under 3 percent for three months or less [12]. A 1999 review estimated that about 6 million Americans and 70 million people worldwide had been exposed and said the long-term prognosis was not known [14]. A review three years after withdrawal described the links with valvular heart disease and primary pulmonary hypertension as clearly established, with some evidence that valve lesions may regress after stopping [13]. A systematic review of drug-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension includes the appetite suppressants, and a 2004 report describes severe multivalvular disease with ergot-derived dopamine agonists [15][16]. A single case report described overdose [18].
Dexfenfluramine promotes release of serotonin and inhibits its reuptake, and its main metabolite is dexnorfenfluramine.[1][2] Its reported elimination half-life is roughly 17-20 hours.[1]

Twenty-two neurologists petitioned the FDA to delay approval, citing animal work on serotonin neuron damage whose methods and conclusions were later questioned.[1] After approval, reports of valve disease emerged, and the FDA announced the withdrawal on 15 September 1997; other markets followed.[1] Sibutramine later filled the niche and was itself removed from the US market in 2010.[1]

Redux was widely prescribed alone and alongside phentermine in the "fen-phen" regimen, according to Grokipedia, which also reports that more than 100 valve cases were recorded, some requiring surgery.[2] Those figures come from an AI-generated reference page and were not checked against primary sources.

According to Wikipedia, more than 50,000 product-liability lawsuits had been filed by 2005, with total liability estimated at up to $14 billion, and Wyeth offered settlements of $5,000 to $200,000 [12]. The episode is widely cited as an example of how efficacy in short trials did not reveal rare heart and lung harms, a point made in a 2023 review of the 5-HT2B receptor in drug discovery [17].

card.summary: The 1990s serotonin diet pill pulled from the market in 1997 after heart-valve and lung-pressure harms.
card.note: Withdrawn worldwide after valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension reports.

quick.overview:
Dexfenfluramine (Redux) was an appetite-suppressing drug approved in the US in the mid-1990s for obesity. Trials showed weight loss with diet, and it was widely prescribed, including with phentermine as fen-phen.

It was withdrawn in September 1997 after valve disease and pulmonary hypertension were reported in users. It is not available today.
quick.mechanism: It raises serotonin signalling in the brain by releasing serotonin and blocking its reuptake, which reduces appetite. Its metabolite also activates 5-HT2B receptors, which researchers link to the heart and lung harms.
quick.risks: Documented harms include heart-valve disease and pulmonary hypertension, which led to withdrawal. It is not marketed anywhere reported in the sources and is not a legitimate option today.

chain: Oral drug raises serotonin signalling in the brain
angle.text: Dexfenfluramine suppressed appetite so that people ate less and lost weight alongside diet and exercise. It was withdrawn in 1997, so it is a historical rather than current route to fat loss.
